summary: Module 5 BREAK (post-incident data loss on top of a breach). The bug is fixed but the damage is done -- this does NOT close the incident; it reclassifies it. My response: (1) Do not declare the incident resolved. A SEV1 breach with confirmed data destruction stays SEV1: severity escalates from 'exposure' to 'confirmed data loss', which triggers breach-notification obligations. (2) Preserve the evidence before touching anything: the audit query is the proof trail (12 rows, 8 accounts, 203.0.113.42, 14:22-14:32 UTC); snapshot the audit output and the DB state so the forensics survive any restore attempt. (3) Establish whether the data is recoverable before promising anything: 'no application-layer backup' does not mean the rows are gone forever -- check the database layer (Postgres WAL/archive, nightly DB dumps, read-replica lag, PITR window) and determine whether a point-in-time restore or WAL replay can recover the 12 rows. Only after that fact-finding can I tell users what happened to their data. (4) Contain and harden, not just the auth bypass: rotate credentials, inspect for other abused paths from 203.0.113.42, and check whether the attacker only deleted or also read -- the same access that deleted rows could have read them, and data loss is the confirmed floor, not the ceiling. (5) Communicate honestly and by tier: leadership gets a SEV1 update stating confirmed data loss, what is recoverable, and the restore plan with an ETA; affected users (the 8 accounts) get individual notification when we know recoverability, not a blanket 'all fine'; no statement to users or VP claims 'it is fine'. The uncomfortable lesson this scenario exists to teach: fixing the door does not bring back what was stolen, and the discipline is to say so plainly while still driving recovery.
evidence: Incident NOT declared closed; reclassified as SEV1 confirmed data loss
Evidence preservation step before any restore attempt
DB-layer recovery check (WAL/PITR) before user-facing promises
Credential rotation + persistence check + read-vs-delete scope expansion
Tiered honest communication: leadership, affected users, no 'it is fine'
